253.title: The body: its parts
253.hook: like a bag of mixed grain opened and looked at: hair, nails, teeth, skin (MN 10)
253.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, the first five parts (hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin) are traditionally taught to new monks and nuns at ordination; the contemplation of the thirty-two parts is recited and practiced to loosen vanity and craving.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sampajanna, clear knowing, and your line was even this. Which chore did you do knowingly? Day two hundred fifty-three.

Think about how much of a day goes into what the body looks like. The mirror in the morning. The photo you retake four times. The comparison that slips in while scrolling. We tend to see the body as one thing, a whole picture, to be judged as good or bad. The Satipatthana Sutta does something different. It opens the body up, piece by piece, with the calm of a farmer checking stored grain. Today: the body, its parts.
screen: `THE MIRROR, THE RETAKEN PHOTO.` → `ONE PICTURE, JUDGED.` → `PIECE BY PIECE.`

segments.voice: The practitioner reviews this very body, the sutta says, from the soles of the feet up and from the top of the head down, bounded by skin and, in the sutta's blunt word, full of many kinds of impurity. Then comes the list: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and on inward, organs and fluids, thirty-one parts in all in the sutta's list. Later tradition added the brain to make thirty-two. And then the image. It's like a bag with an opening at both ends, full of mixed grain: hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, sesame, husked rice. A person with good eyes opens it and looks: this is rice, these are beans, this is sesame. Notice the tone. The person with the grain bag isn't disgusted, and isn't admiring. They're just sorting, clearly. That's the heart of the practice. In the Buddhist tradition, this contemplation is used to loosen two strong pulls: vanity about the body and craving for other bodies. Some teachers stress the unattractiveness of the parts; others, especially today, stress simple, neutral seeing. Either way, the point is not to hate the body. It's to see it as it is: not a single image to be judged, but a working collection of many things, all doing their jobs. Hair is hair. Teeth are teeth. The picture in the mirror loosens its grip a little.
screen: `FROM THE SOLES UP, THE HEAD DOWN.` · `HAIR, NAILS, TEETH, SKIN.` · `A BAG OF MIXED GRAIN, OPENED.` · `SORTING, NOT JUDGING.` · then, large: `A BAG OF GRAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Name ten parts of your body, slowly, feeling each one if you can, with the calm of someone sorting grain. Hair. Nails. Teeth. Skin. Bones. Muscles. Heart. Lungs. Blood. Breath. No judging any of them, no admiring or wincing. Just this is that. If any part is painful or hard to think about today, skip it gently and move on. The bell holds the time.
The body, its parts. Opened like a bag of mixed grain and sorted calmly: hair, nails, teeth, skin, each one just what it is.
Your line: a bag of grain. Today, when the mirror starts judging, try sorting instead: skin, hair, eyes, each one just doing its job. Day two hundred fifty-three.

pairs: hill rice, red rice, beans, sesame
the count once the brain is added

it's for seeing clearly and loosening vanity and craving, not for self-hatred.
the sutta's list has thirty-one parts; later tradition added the brain
the familiar count of thirty-two comes from the later list.
the grain simile is about sorting calmly
the person just sees: this is rice, these are beans.

fork.setup: you open a bag of mixed grain. what does the person in the sutta do?
options: throw it out in disgust.
look and sort: this is rice, these are beans.
admire how beautiful the grain is.
fork.reveal: the person with good eyes simply sees each thing for what it is. the body is looked at the same way.

trapdoor: what you thought: this practice is about finding the body gross.
what it means: seeing the body clearly as many parts, not one image to judge.
what a scholar hears: MN 10 lists thirty-one parts; the Khuddakapāṭha and later texts add the brain (matthaluṅga) to make thirty-two, and the first five are taught at ordination.

254.title: The body: elements
254.hook: like a butcher who has divided a carcass: earth, water, fire, air (MN 10)
254.howItsDone: Meditators in several Buddhist traditions practice elements meditation by feeling hardness, cohesion, heat and motion in the body; in some Burmese and Thai lineages it is a core practice for seeing the body as not-self.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, its parts, sorted like a bag of grain. Did the mirror judge less, or sort more? Day two hundred fifty-four, and the body again, from a new angle.

Put your hand flat on a table. Notice the hardness under your palm. Now notice the warmth of your own hand, and maybe a slight dampness. Notice the tiny movements: the pulse, the breath shifting your shoulders. Hard, wet, warm, moving. Before anyone had a microscope, people across the ancient world sorted everything they touched into a few basic kinds like these. The Satipatthana Sutta uses that old sorting to look at the body in a way that's surprisingly freeing. Today: the body, elements.
screen: `HARD, WET, WARM, MOVING.` → `AN OLD WAY OF SORTING.` → `THE BODY AS ELEMENTS.`

segments.voice: The sutta says the practitioner reviews this very body, however it is placed, however it is disposed, by way of the elements. In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element. In Pali each is a dhatu, an element, and in Buddhist teaching they're less like substances and more like qualities you can feel. Earth is hardness and solidity: bones, teeth, the weight in your seat. Water is cohesion and fluidity: blood, sweat, the way things hold together. Fire is heat: warmth, digestion, the fever and the chill. Air is movement: the breath, the pulse, the push and pull inside. Then the image, and it's a blunt one. It's like a skilled butcher, or his apprentice, who has killed a cow and divided it at a crossroads, sitting with it cut into portions. The point of the picture is the change in how you see. Before, you'd call it a cow. Now it's portions of meat for sale. The name has fallen away, and what's left is just what's there. Looking at the body by elements does the same thing to the word me. Instead of a single, solid self, you find hardness, fluid, warmth and motion, the same four that are in the table, the rain, the sun and the wind. It isn't cold. Many people find it a relief: the body is made of the world, and belongs to it.
screen: `DHATU: EARTH, WATER, FIRE, AIR.` · `QUALITIES YOU CAN FEEL.` · `THE BUTCHER AT THE CROSSROADS.` · `THE BODY IS MADE OF THE WORLD.` · then, large: `FOUR ELEMENTS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Feel earth: the solidness where you sit, the weight of your hands. Feel water: the moisture in your mouth, the way the body holds together. Feel fire: the warmth of your hands, or a cool spot on your skin. Feel air: the breath moving, the pulse if you can find it. Solid, fluid, warm, moving. Then rest in all four at once, and let the word me soften a little. The bell holds the time.
The body, elements. Earth, water, fire and air: hardness, fluid, warmth and motion, the same four that make up the world.
Your line: four elements. Today, as you drink something, feel the four at once: the cup's hardness, the liquid, its warmth or cold, and the swallow moving. Day two hundred fifty-four.

what a scholar hears: the commentaries explain the butcher simile through the name falling away: before cutting, the perception is 'cow'; afterward, only 'meat'.

255.title: The body: the charnel ground
255.hook: a body one day dead, two days, three; this body too is of that nature (MN 10), offered gently
255.howItsDone: Reflection on death (maranasati) is practiced across Buddhist traditions; in Thailand and Sri Lanka some monastics still contemplate bodies or skeletons, while most lay practitioners reflect quietly that this body, too, will not last.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, as four elements: earth, water, fire, air. Did you feel all four in one drink? Day two hundred fifty-five, the last exercise on the body.

A quick word before today. The last body exercise in the sutta is about death, and it's direct. If you're grieving right now, or today just isn't the day, it's completely fine to listen lightly, or to spend the practice with your breath instead. Nothing is lost. For everyone else: most of us live as if our own body were the one exception. Other people get old. Other people die. Somehow, not quite me. The sutta asks us to look at that gently, and honestly. Today: the body, the charnel ground.
screen: `A GENTLE NOTE FIRST.` → `THE ONE EXCEPTION.` → `THE CHARNEL GROUND.`

segments.voice: In ancient India, a charnel ground was a place outside town where bodies were left, rather than buried or burned. Monks and nuns sometimes went there to practice. The sutta describes a practitioner who sees a body there: one day dead, two days, three. Then, over nine stages, it describes what happens next, until at last there are only scattered bones, bleached white, and finally bones crumbled to dust. At each stage the practitioner turns to their own body and reflects: this body too is of the same nature. It will become like that. It is not exempt. That's the line the whole exercise rests on: this body too. It sounds grim, but look at what it's for. It isn't meant to frighten, or to make life feel worthless. In Buddhist teaching, remembering death, maranasati, is meant to wake you up to what matters. The Buddha is remembered as saying that mindfulness of death, well practiced, is of great fruit. If this body won't last forever, then the call you keep postponing matters. The grudge you're carrying weighs more than it's worth. And the ordinary morning you're living right now is precious, exactly because it's passing. Many practitioners say this reflection, done gently, leaves them calmer, not sadder. The fear of death is often loudest when we refuse to look at it. And notice: the chorus comes back even here. Arising and passing away. The body is the clearest example there is.
screen: `A CHARNEL GROUND OUTSIDE TOWN.` · `NINE STAGES, DOWN TO DUST.` · `IT IS NOT EXEMPT.` · `REMEMBERING DEATH WAKES YOU UP.` · then, large: `THIS BODY TOO.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and feel your body breathing. It's alive, warm, working. Quietly, if it feels right, reflect: this body too will not last forever. Let the thought be soft, not frightening. Then ask one question: given that, what matters today? Let an answer come, or not. If this feels too heavy right now, just rest with the breath instead. The bell holds the time.
The body, the charnel ground. Seeing another body return to dust, the practitioner reflects: this body too is of that nature.
Your line: this body too. Today, do one thing you've been putting off because you assumed there'd always be time. Day two hundred fifty-five.

from one day dead to dust

it's meant to wake you up to what matters, because life is passing.
the sutta describes nine stages, ending with bones crumbled to dust
at each stage the practitioner reflects: this body too.

fork.reveal: at every stage the practitioner applies what they see to their own body: it will become like that; it is not exempt.

what it means: seeing gently that this body too will pass, so today matters.
what a scholar hears: MN 10 gives nine charnel-ground contemplations (sīvathikā); the Buddha's praise of maraṇasati as 'of great fruit' is in AN 6.19–20.

256.title: Feelings
256.hook: pleasant, painful, neither; worldly and unworldly (MN 10)
256.howItsDone: Many insight meditation teachers have students note the feeling tone of experiences as pleasant, unpleasant or neutral, since Buddhist teaching places vedana just before craving in the chain of dependent origination.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, the charnel ground, and your line: this body too. Did you do the thing you'd been putting off? Day two hundred fifty-six, and the second foundation.

Before you know what something is, you already know whether you like it. A song starts, and before you can name it, something in you has leaned in or pulled back. A smell drifts out of a kitchen: yes, or no. A text lights up your phone, and there's a little flicker of good or bad before you've read a word. That flicker is so fast we barely see it, and it steers almost everything we do next. The Satipatthana Sutta makes it the second foundation. Today's word: vedana.
screen: `BEFORE YOU KNOW WHAT IT IS.` → `A FLICKER: YES OR NO.` → `THE SECOND FOUNDATION.`

segments.voice: Vedana is usually translated feeling, but it doesn't mean emotions like joy or anger. It means the feeling tone of any experience: pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful. Every sight, sound, smell, taste, touch and thought comes with one of the three. The sutta's instruction is simple. When feeling a pleasant feeling, the practitioner knows, I feel a pleasant feeling. When feeling a painful feeling, they know it. When feeling one that's neither, they know that too. Then a second layer. Each feeling can be worldly or unworldly. Worldly feelings are tied to ordinary things: the pleasure of good food, the pain of an insult. Unworldly ones come from practice itself: the quiet joy of a calm mind, or the ache of wanting to be free. And then, of course, the chorus: inside, outside, arising and passing away. Why does this get a whole foundation? Because in Buddhist teaching, feeling is the hinge. In the chain the Buddha called dependent origination, feeling gives rise to craving. Pleasant feeling tends to spark wanting more. Painful feeling tends to spark pushing away. Neutral feeling tends to spark boredom, and we drift off looking for something more interesting. If you can catch the feeling while it's still just a feeling, before it becomes a want or a push, you've found a gap. And in that gap, you get a choice.
screen: `NOT EMOTION: FEELING TONE.` · `PLEASANT, PAINFUL, NEITHER.` · `WORLDLY AND UNWORLDLY.` · `FEELING IS THE HINGE TO CRAVING.` · then, large: `PLEASANT, PAINFUL, NEITHER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your attention move around the body and the room. Each time something catches you, a sound, an ache, the warmth of your hands, a thought, give it one quiet label: pleasant, painful, or neither. Don't explain it. Don't change it. Just label and let it go. You may notice how many things are simply neither. That's normal. The bell holds the time.
Vedana. The feeling tone of every experience: pleasant, painful, or neither. The hinge between what happens and what we want.
Your line: pleasant, painful, neither. Today, when you reach for your phone, catch the feeling tone just before you reach. Name it. Day two hundred fifty-six.

pairs: the quiet joy of a calm mind
most small moments of the day

it means feeling tone: pleasant, painful, or neither.
in dependent origination, feeling gives rise to craving
that's why catching the feeling opens a gap.
the sutta divides feelings into worldly and unworldly too
tied to ordinary things, or arising from practice itself.

fork.setup: you taste something delicious and immediately reach for more. where in that moment does the sutta suggest looking?
options: at the recipe.
at the pleasant feeling itself, before the reach.
at whether you deserve it.
fork.reveal: knowing the pleasant feeling as a feeling, before craving takes over, is the whole second foundation.

original.note: Pali vedanā: feeling tone, pleasant, painful or neither.

trapdoor: what you thought: vedana means your emotions.
what it means: the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of every experience.
what a scholar hears: in the twelve links of dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda), contact conditions vedanā, and vedanā conditions taṇhā, craving.

257.title: The second arrow
257.hook: pain is one arrow; the distress we add is a second (SN 36.6)
257.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers of many schools use the two arrows image from the Sallatha Sutta, and it is widely used in pain care and mindfulness courses to separate physical pain from the distress added to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vedana, feeling tone. Your line: pleasant, painful, neither. Did you catch the feeling before you reached for your phone? Day two hundred fifty-seven.

You stub your toe on the bed frame at night. There's the pain, sharp and real. And then, within a second: who put this bed here, why am I so clumsy, this always happens to me, now I'll never get back to sleep. The toe hurt for thirty seconds. The rest of it went on for twenty minutes. The Buddha has a short teaching about exactly this, and it's one of the most useful ideas in the whole tradition. Today: the second arrow.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE AT NIGHT.` → `THIRTY SECONDS OF PAIN.` → `TWENTY MINUTES OF THE REST.`

segments.voice: The teaching is in the Connected Discourses, a sutta called the Arrow. The Buddha asks his monks a question. When an ordinary person and a well-trained disciple both feel pain, what's the difference? Then he answers with an image. An untrained person, touched by a painful feeling, worries, grieves, laments, beats their chest and becomes distraught. It's as if they were struck by an arrow, and then struck by a second arrow right after. They feel two pains: one in the body, one in the mind. The well-trained disciple, touched by the same painful feeling, doesn't add the worry and the lament. They are struck by one arrow, and not by a second. They feel one pain, the bodily one, and not the other. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. He doesn't say the trained person feels no pain. The first arrow lands on everyone, including, in the texts, the Buddha himself, who had backaches and grew old. The teaching is only about the second arrow, the one we fire at ourselves. And he adds something sharp. When pain comes, the untrained person often runs toward sensual pleasure to escape it, because they know no other way out. That's a third trap, hidden inside the second. This links straight back to yesterday. Pain is a feeling, vedana. The second arrow is what we do next. If you can see the feeling as just a feeling, you've stopped the second arrow before it leaves the bow.
screen: `THE ARROW SUTTA.` · `STRUCK BY ONE, THEN BY A SECOND.` · `THE FIRST ARROW LANDS ON EVERYONE.` · `THE SECOND IS THE ONE WE FIRE.` · then, large: `ONE ARROW, NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and find some small discomfort: a stiff knee, an itch, a tight shoulder, or a worry you've been carrying. Feel the first arrow: just the raw sensation, or the plain fact. Then watch for the second arrow: the story, the complaint, the why me. When you notice it, name it quietly: second arrow. Then return to the first, and let it be only what it is. The bell holds the time.
The second arrow. Pain is the first arrow, and it lands on everyone. The distress we add on top is the second, and we fire it ourselves.
Your line: one arrow, not two. Today, when something goes wrong, catch one second arrow before it lands, and say to yourself: one arrow, not two. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

the first arrow lands on everyone; the teaching is about the second.
the Buddha himself is said to have had physical pain
the texts mention his backaches and old age.
the second arrow is the distress we add on top
worry, grieving, lamenting: a second pain in the mind.

original.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart; the sutta's name is Sallatha, the arrow.

trapdoor: what you thought: the second arrow means a second bad thing happening.
what it means: the distress we add to pain: the story, the worry, the lament.
what a scholar hears: SN 36.6 adds that the untrained person, not knowing any escape from pain except sensual pleasure, is drawn to it, so the latent tendency to lust also grows.

258.title: The mind
258.hook: a mind with lust or without, with hate or without, contracted or scattered (MN 10)
258.howItsDone: In contemplation of mind, practitioners periodically note the overall quality of the mind, such as agitated, calm, dull or clear, including the absence of a state, without trying to change it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the second arrow. Your line was one arrow, not two. Did you catch one before it landed? Day two hundred fifty-eight, and the third foundation.
screen: `THE SECOND ARROW — ONE ARROW, NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Someone asks how you are, and you say fine. But what's the weather in there, really? Foggy? Stormy? Bright but a little windy? Most of us are so busy with what's on our minds, the email, the argument, the list, that we never notice the mind itself: its mood, its shape, its temperature. It's like reading every word on a page without ever noticing the color of the paper. The third foundation in the Satipatthana Sutta asks you to notice the paper. Today's word: citta, the mind.
screen: `'FINE.' BUT WHAT'S THE WEATHER?` → `WHAT'S ON THE MIND, NOT THE MIND.` → `NOTICE THE PAPER.`

segments.voice: Citta is the Pali word for mind, or heart; the tradition doesn't split them the way English does. The sutta gives a list of pairs, and for each one the instruction is the same: know it. A mind with lust, know it as a mind with lust. A mind without lust, know it as without. A mind with hate, or without hate. A mind with delusion, or without. Then the list goes on. A contracted mind, pulled in and sluggish, or a scattered one, flying in all directions. An exalted mind, lifted by deep meditation, or one that isn't. A surpassable mind, or unsurpassable. A concentrated mind, or not. A liberated mind, or not yet. Sixteen states in all, in eight pairs. Notice two things. First, the list includes the good states too. You know a calm mind as calm, not only an agitated one as agitated. This isn't a search for faults. It's a weather report, sunny days included. Second, every pair includes the absence. A mind without anger is worth noticing. We usually only notice anger when it shows up; we rarely notice the quiet hour when it's gone. That noticing is its own small gladness. And the chorus returns: inside and outside, arising and passing away. Mind states come and go just like breaths. The fog lifts. The storm passes. And simply knowing the weather already changes how you stand in it.
screen: `CITTA: MIND AND HEART TOGETHER.` · `WITH LUST OR WITHOUT, HATE OR WITHOUT.` · `CONTRACTED OR SCATTERED.` · `NOTICE THE ABSENCE TOO.` · then, large: `KNOW THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and take three slow breaths. Then ask: what's the mind like right now? Not what's on it: what's it like? Tight or open? Scattered or gathered? Irritated, or free of irritation? Heavy or light? Pick one plain word for it, and hold that word lightly. As the minutes pass, check again. Has the weather shifted? The bell holds the time.
Citta. The mind and heart together: its states, its weather, known as they are, whether stormy or clear.
Your line: know the mind. Today, three times, name your mind's state in one word, and once, notice something that isn't there, like a worry that's gone quiet. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

the list includes calm, concentrated and liberated minds too: a full weather report.
the sutta asks you to notice when anger is absent
every pair includes the absence: a mind without hate, known as without.
citta covers both mind and heart
Pali doesn't split them the way English does.

options: ignore it; only problems need attention.

trapdoor: what you thought: contemplating the mind means thinking about your thoughts.
what it means: noticing the mind's overall state, its weather, including what's absent.

259.title: Knowing without fixing
259.hook: you know an angry mind as angry: that is the whole instruction
259.howItsDone: Insight meditation teachers often stress bare knowing of mind states, noting 'angry' or 'restless' without judgment, as the first step; remedies such as loving-kindness are taught separately.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was citta, the mind, and your line was know the mind. Did you notice a worry that had gone quiet? Day two hundred fifty-nine, the end of another week in the sutta.

You notice you're anxious. Right away, a whole repair crew shows up. You should calm down. Why are you like this? Try breathing slower. Think positive. Fix it, fix it, fix it. And somehow, the anxiety gets worse, now with a layer of frustration on top. Anyone who has ever been told to relax knows how well that works. Yesterday's list in the sutta had an instruction hiding in it that's so simple it's easy to miss. Today: knowing without fixing.
screen: `THE REPAIR CREW SHOWS UP.` → `'JUST RELAX.'` → `AN INSTRUCTION HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Look again at how the sutta words it. A mind with anger: know it as a mind with anger. That's all. It doesn't say, then remove the anger. It doesn't say, replace it with kindness. It doesn't say, feel bad for being angry. In this section, the whole instruction is to know. Other teachings in the Buddhist tradition do give remedies: kindness for ill will, reflection for craving, and we'll meet those. But the Satipatthana Sutta puts something first. Before you change anything, see it clearly. Here's why that matters. The moment we try to fix a mind state, we're usually pushing against it, and pushing is its own kind of aversion. It's the second arrow again, aimed at our own moods. Knowing, on the other hand, takes a step back. When you say, this is an angry mind, you're no longer just angry. You're also the one who sees the anger. There's a little space there, and in that space the anger often loosens by itself, the way a knot loosens when you stop pulling both ends. Look back over this week and you'll see the same move everywhere. The parts of the body, sorted like grain. The elements, felt as they are. The charnel ground: this body too. Feelings: pleasant, painful, neither. The second arrow, not fired. The mind, known as the weather. Every one of them is seeing, not fixing. That's the week's real lesson.
screen: `A MIND WITH ANGER: KNOW IT.` · `SEE CLEARLY BEFORE CHANGING.` · `FIXING IS OFTEN PUSHING.` · `THE WEEK: SEEING, NOT FIXING.` · then, large: `JUST KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Find whatever mood is here right now: restless, flat, content, tired, a little sad. Name it plainly: a restless mind. Then, instead of fixing it, just stay with it, the way you'd sit with a friend who doesn't need advice. If the urge to fix it shows up, know that too: a mind that wants to fix. Nothing to do but know. The bell holds the time.
